 The ‘maniac dance’ first mentioned in l. 110, and described in detail in ll. 137–60, pro-
vides a good case study of S.’s syncretic use of source material. The behaviour of the dancers
around the triumph strongly resembles the ecstatic worship of Ancient Greece, and the
demeanour of those at ll. 147 and 165–7 shows the influence of the Bacchae of Euripides
(one of the Greek tragedians S. was reading carefully in late 1821; see headnote to An archer
stood upon the Tower of Babel (Longman v, no. 414)). S. is also drawing from his own
